title: 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami
description: Megathrust earthquake off Japan's east coast
wiki_lead:
On 11 March 2011, at 14:46:24 local time (UTC+9), a Mw 9.0–9.1 undersea megathrust earthquake occurred in the Pacific Ocean, 72 km (45 mi) east of the Oshika Peninsula of the Tōhoku region of Japan. It lasted approximately six minutes and caused a tsunami. It is sometimes known in Japan as the "Great East Japan Earthquake" (東日本大震災, Higashi Nihon Daishinsai), among other names. It is often referred to by its numerical date, 3.11 (read San ten Ichi-ichi in Japanese).
The earthquake was the most powerful ever recorded in Japan, and the fourth most powerful recorded in the world since modern seismography began in 1900. It triggered powerful tsunami waves that may have reached heights of up to 40.5 m (133 ft) in Miyako in Tōhoku's Iwate Prefecture, and which, in the Sendai area, traveled at 700 km/h (435 mph) and up to 10 km (6 mi) inland. Residents of Sendai had only eight to ten minutes of warning, and more than a hundred evacuation sites were washed away. The snowfall which accompanied the tsunami and the freezing temperature hindered rescue works; for instance, in Ishinomaki, the city with the most deaths, the temperature was 0 °C (32 °F) as the tsunami hit. Official figures released in 2021 reported 19,759 deaths, 6,242 injured, 284 firefighters dead from attempts to close preventative fire gates, and 2,553 missing. A report in 2015 found that 228,863 people were still living away from their home either temporarily or permanently.
The tsunami caused the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, primarily the meltdowns of three of its reactors, the discharge of radioactive water in Fukushima and the associated evacuation zones affecting hundreds of thousands of residents. Many electrical generators ran out of fuel. The loss of electrical power halted cooling systems, causing heat to build. Without ventilation, hydrogen gas accumulated within the upper refueling hall and exploded, forcefully ejecting the refueling hall's blast panels. Residents within a 20 km (12 mi) radius of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant and a 10 km (6.2 mi) radius of the Fukushima Daini Nuclear Power Plant were evacuated.
Early estimates placed insured losses from the earthquake alone at US$14.5 to $34.6 billion. The Bank of Japan offered ¥15 trillion (US$183 billion) to the banking system on 14 March 2011 in an effort to normalize market conditions. The estimated economic damage amounted to over $300 billion, making it the costliest natural disaster in history. According to a 2020 study, "the earthquake and its aftermaths resulted in a 0.47-percentage-point decline in Japan's real GDP growth in the year following the disaster".

grok_lead: The 2011 TÅhoku earthquake and tsunami, also known as the Great East Japan Earthquake or the Japan Earthquake and Tsunami in 2011, was a magnitude 9.1 undersea megathrust earthquake that occurred at 14:46 JST (05:46 UTC) on March 11, 2011, with its epicenter approximately 70 km east of the Oshika Peninsula off the northeastern coast of Honshu, Japan. The rupture propagated along the Japan Trench subduction zone, where the Pacific Plate thrusts beneath the Okhotsk Plate, releasing energy equivalent to over 400 megatons of TNT and shifting the Japanese main island eastward by up to 2.4 meters. This event, the strongest recorded in Japanese history, triggered a tsunami with maximum run-up heights of 40.5 meters in Miyako, Iwate Prefecture. The tsunami waves, arriving within 30 minutes along the Pacific coast, inundated over 560 square kilometers of land, destroying infrastructure, homes, and fisheries in the TÅhoku region. Official records indicate 15,901 confirmed deaths and 2,519 persons missing as of March 2026, with nearly all fatalities attributed to drowning from the tsunami rather than shaking. Economic losses exceeded 220 billion USD, marking it as one of the costliest natural disasters globally. The disaster also precipitated the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident, where tsunami flooding disabled cooling systems at three reactors, leading to meltdowns, hydrogen explosions, and the release of radioactive materials. Seismic activity included intense ground shakingâreaching intensity 7 on Japan's scale in Miyagi Prefecture âand widespread aftershocks, including several exceeding magnitude 7.0. The event highlighted vulnerabilities in tsunami preparedness, as waves overtopped many seawalls designed for lower heights based on historical precedents, prompting revisions to hazard models and infrastructure standards.
